transcript.text: Bit of a weird one - my son put the microwave on for 10 minutes with nothing in it by accident. Now there's a horrible smell. Is it broken?

Not a weird question at all. It's a fairly common accident. Running a microwave empty is one of the worse things you can do to it, but 10 minutes doesn't automatically mean it's broken.

Why it's a problem
Normally the food or liquid absorbs the microwave energy. With nothing inside, the energy bounces around and gets reflected back into the magnetron (the part that generates the microwaves), which can overheat it. Many modern microwaves have thermal cut-outs to protect against this, so it may have survived fine.

What the smell might be
• Burnt food residue: Old splatters on the walls or ceiling can get scorched. This is the most common and harmless cause.
• The waveguide cover: A small rectangular panel (often mica or cardboard-like) on the inside wall. If it has grease on it, it can burn or even spark.
• Overheated internal components: A sharper, electrical or "hot plastic" smell suggests something inside got very hot.

What to do now
1. Unplug it and let it cool completely, at least 30 to 60 minutes.
2. Look inside: Check for scorch marks, melted bits, or damage to the waveguide cover.
3. Clean and air it out: Wipe the interior, then microwave a bowl of water with a few slices of lemon or a splash of vinegar for 3 to 5 minutes. This helps with lingering odours.
4. Test it: Heat a mug of water for 1 minute. If the water gets properly hot and the microwave sounds and behaves normally, it's very likely fine.

Stop using it if you notice:
• Sparking or arcing inside
• Water not heating (or only barely warming)
• Unusual buzzing, humming, or grinding noises
• A burning or electrical smell that comes back during normal use
• Visible damage or melting

If any of those happen, it's probably time for a repair or replacement. Don't open the casing yourself, as microwaves contain a capacitor that can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged.

A handy tip for the future: leaving a cup of water inside when it's not in use means an accidental start won't run it empty.

There was actually a bit of smoke coming out of the vents at the side when I opened the door, and the smell is a hot electrical, burnt sort of smell. I've turned it off at the switch but it's still plugged in. Is it safe to try the water test?

No, don't do the water test. Smoke from the side vents plus a hot electrical smell means something inside the casing overheated, not just food residue in the cooking area. Running it again could cause further damage or a fire.

What to do now
1. Unplug it. It's off at the switch, so it's safe to pull the plug. If the plug or socket feels hot or looks scorched, switch off that circuit at the fuse box first if you can.
2. Keep the door closed and leave it to cool. Open a window to air out the room.
3. Watch it for a while. If smoke keeps coming out, or you see flames or glowing inside, leave the door shut (that starves a fire of oxygen), keep everyone away, and call the fire brigade if it doesn't stop quickly.
4. Don't open the casing. Even unplugged, the high-voltage capacitor inside can hold a dangerous charge.

What next
The magnetron or another internal component has likely been damaged. Your options:
• Under warranty? Contact the manufacturer or retailer before doing anything else.
• Repair: A qualified appliance technician can check it, though for most standard microwaves the repair cost is close to or more than a new one.
• Replace: Often the simplest choice. Take the old one to a recycling centre or electrical waste collection rather than putting it in household rubbish.

It's a shame, but you've done the right thing by stopping and checking rather than carrying on using it.
